topics.framing_note: Framework names 'Turner, Delacroix's Liberty Leading the People.' Pillar-1 19th-c thread — emotion and color over Neoclassical order. Cool-fact hooks: Liberty as a bare-breasted allegory striding over the barricade dead (often miscalled a French Revolution scene — it's 1830); Turner reportedly lashing himself to a ship's mast to paint a real snowstorm. Ask the specific.

topics.name: Impressionism — Monet and the movement
topics.scope: Impression Sunrise; plein air; water lilies; broken color
topics.source: Core Knowledge; AP Art History; cultural literacy
topics.framing_note: The break into modern art — Pillar-1 keystone. Surprise-reversal hook (§2): 'Impressionism' began as an INSULT from a hostile critic mocking Monet's 'Impression, Sunrise'; the painters kept the slur as their name. Plein-air = made possible by the new portable paint tube (ordinary-ingenuity mechanism). Cool-fact answer over 'who painted.'

topics.name: Van Gogh — Starry Night and the ear
topics.scope: Post-Impressionist; sold one painting; cut his ear; suicide
topics.source: Core Knowledge modern American/European; cultural literacy
topics.framing_note: Framework names 'Van Gogh (Starry Night, ear).' Tortured-genius archetype = drama-of-the-mind at a kid-accessible level. Honest, not theatricalized (§4): the ear and the suicide are stated as fact, not staged as a reveal; sold essentially one painting alive yet now among the most famous painters ever = surprise-reversal. Starry Night painted from a sanatorium window. Mind the strict drama-available rule — ask about the act, not a venue/date.

topics.name: Picasso and Cubism
topics.scope: Les Demoiselles; Guernica; fractured multiple viewpoints
topics.source: Core Knowledge modern art; AP Art History; cultural literacy
topics.framing_note: Framework names 'Picasso's Guernica 1937 (response to the German bombing).' High weight — modern-art revolution AND a moral-witness painting against the bombing of civilians (fits the bank's honest-about-atrocity stance). Cubism = showing multiple viewpoints at once is the mechanism hook. The legend of Picasso telling a Nazi officer 'No, YOU did' about Guernica is the cool-fact answer. Distinguish classic Picasso from any modern-slop framing.

topics.name: Rodin and modern sculpture — The Thinker
topics.scope: Rodin's Thinker and Burghers of Calais
topics.framing_note: Gateway to modern sculpture. Cool-fact answer: The Thinker was originally a small figure of the poet Dante perched atop the Gates of Hell, brooding over the damned, before being enlarged into a standalone icon. The Burghers of Calais set at ground level (no heroic pedestal) so the viewer meets the condemned men eye to eye = the deliberate anti-monument wonder. (Note: consensus title mis-tags 'Monet'; topic is Rodin.)

topics.name: Surrealism — Dali's melting clocks
topics.scope: Persistence of Memory; dream imagery
topics.framing_note: Modern-movement keystone kids recognize. Cool-fact hook: Dali said the soft melting watches came from staring at a runny Camembert cheese; the dreamlike imagery is the draw. Keep it on the art/mechanism level; avoid any current-politics or edgy-biography drift. Ask the specific, not attribution.

topics.name: American modern art — Hopper, Pollock, Warhol
topics.scope: Nighthawks; drip painting; pop-art soup cans
topics.source: Core Knowledge American art; cultural literacy
topics.framing_note: 20th-c American contribution — fits the celebrate-the-American-experiment thread (moral_vision §2/§3.6) at the cultural level. Cool-fact answers: Pollock's drip technique = painting with the canvas on the FLOOR, walking around it, never touching brush to cloth; Hopper's Nighthawks diner with no visible door; Warhol's exactly-32 soup-can canvases for the 32 varieties. Present straight; no ideology.

topics.name: Lascaux / Altamira cave paintings
topics.scope: Paleolithic animal paintings; discovered by accident
topics.source: AP Art History (Global Prehistory); Core Knowledge
topics.framing_note: The origin of human art — pure wonder (§2): humans 17,000+ years ago made deliberate beautiful images. Cool-fact answer: Lascaux found in 1940 by four teenagers and a dog chasing a rabbit down a hole; Altamira's bison so sophisticated that scholars first dismissed them as a hoax — too good to be 'primitive.' That dismissal-then-vindication is the surprise-reversal. NO condescension to the past (§4).

topics.name: Egyptian art and the pyramids of Giza
topics.scope: profile convention; Great Pyramid; Sphinx; King Tut's mask
topics.source: Core Knowledge ancient Egypt; AP Art History; cultural literacy
topics.framing_note: Monumental ancient art every kid knows — present on its own terms (§4, no exotic-foil framing). Framework names 'Tutankhamun's tomb discovered by Carter 1922 (yes, wonderful things).' That quote is the Tier-1 Named-Things answer. Cool-fact: the strict profile-convention (head and legs sideways, eye and shoulders front) held for 3,000 years; the Great Pyramid was the tallest human structure for ~3,800 years.

topics.name: Illuminated manuscripts (Book of Kells / Lindisfarne)
topics.scope: hand-painted gospels; monastic gold-leaf labor
topics.source: Core Knowledge medieval; AP Art History
topics.framing_note: How books were art before printing — DIRECTLY the moral_vision §3.4 thread (the unnamed monks who copied through plague years, §2 'courage in pursuit of truth'). Framework names Book of Kells + Lindisfarne Gospels. Cool-fact answer: a single carpet-page could take a monk months, with pigment ground from lapis lazuli traded all the way from Afghanistan. Sets up the Gutenberg contrast. Christian heritage on its own terms.

topics.name: Gutenberg's printing press and the printed book
topics.scope: movable type ~1450; 42-line Bible; idea revolution
topics.source: Core Knowledge; AP Euro; cultural literacy
topics.framing_note: THE ideas-revolution keystone of the strand — mass literacy, the information revolution of its age, the engine of the Reformation that follows. High weight. Framework names 'Gutenberg's 42-line Bible 1450 (the first printed Bible).' Cool-fact answers: movable metal type let one press do the work of dozens of scribes; he went bankrupt and lost the business to his investor Fust before the Bibles even sold. Celebrate the real human progress.

topics.name: Islamic art and architecture (Alhambra / Dome of the Rock)
topics.scope: arabesque; geometric tile; calligraphy; no figures
topics.source: Core Knowledge Islamic art (explicit); AP World; AP Art History
topics.framing_note: Non-Western tradition ON ITS OWN TERMS (§4, NOT exotic foil) — the aniconic tradition of pattern and calligraphy. Cool-fact answer: because figural images were avoided in sacred art, Islamic artists pushed geometry and calligraphy to dazzling heights — Alhambra tilework contains nearly all the mathematically possible symmetry patterns centuries before mathematicians catalogued them. Framework's honest decline-thread (al-Ghazali) belongs in context, not as the art's framing. Honest comparison is not condescension.

topics.name: Great Mosque of Cordoba
topics.scope: horseshoe arches; Moorish Spain; mosque-cathedral
topics.framing_note: Iconic Islamic-Spain architecture, on its own terms. Cool-fact answer: the forest of double-tier red-and-white horseshoe arches (over 850 columns) creating an endless-hall illusion; a Renaissance cathedral was later built right into its center, and Charles V reportedly regretted it ('you have destroyed something unique'). The mosque-then-cathedral layering is stated as historical fact, no editorial.

topics.name: Taj Mahal
topics.scope: Mughal marble tomb 1632-53; Shah Jahan for Mumtaz
topics.source: AP World; AP Art History anchor work; cultural literacy
topics.framing_note: Framework names 'Taj Mahal 1632-53 (Shah Jahan for Mumtaz).' Mughal achievement on its own terms — the love-story monument. Cool-fact answers: built as a tomb for the wife who died bearing their 14th child; the perfect symmetry broken only by Shah Jahan's own later-added tomb beside hers; inlaid with semi-precious stones that glow at dawn. Present straight as a world masterpiece.

topics.name: Chinese art — landscape painting, calligraphy, porcelain
topics.scope: ink landscapes; the brush; blue-and-white porcelain
topics.source: Core Knowledge Chinese art (explicit); AP World
topics.framing_note: Major non-Western tradition on its own terms (§4) — the brush and the ceramic. Cool-fact answers: a master ink landscape leaves vast areas of blank silk as mist and water, where what's NOT painted carries the scene; blue-and-white porcelain was so prized that 'china' became the English word for all fine ceramic. Substantive civilization, not exotic foil.

topics.name: Terracotta Army of Qin Shi Huang
topics.scope: 8,000 unique clay soldiers buried; discovered 1974
topics.framing_note: Framework names 'Qin Shi Huang + terracotta army.' Staggering ancient sculpture program — vivid kid hook. Cool-fact answer: every one of the ~8,000 soldiers has a DIFFERENT face, as if modeled on real men; found in 1974 by farmers digging a well; they were originally painted in bright colors that flaked away within minutes of hitting the air. On its own terms, no exotic framing.

topics.name: Japanese art — Hokusai's Great Wave and woodblock prints
topics.scope: ukiyo-e; the Great Wave; influence on Impressionists
topics.source: Core Knowledge Japanese art (explicit); AP Art History
topics.framing_note: Non-Western tradition on its own terms PLUS the East-to-West influence thread the framework prizes (these prints shaped Monet/Van Gogh — connects to the Impressionism cell). Cool-fact answer: the tiny Mount Fuji sitting calm in the distance UNDER the towering claw of the wave; mass-produced cheap woodblock prints, not elite paintings, that ended up remaking European art. Ask the specific.

topics.name: African art — Benin bronzes and masks
topics.scope: lost-wax bronze plaques; ritual masks; looted 1897
topics.source: Core Knowledge African art (explicit); AP Art History (Africa)
topics.framing_note: Sophisticated metalwork tradition on its own terms — celebrate the achievement (the lost-wax casting rivaled anything in Europe, shattering the 'primitive Africa' myth). The honest record (framework Pillar 5): the bronzes were looted in the 1897 British Punitive Expedition, whose altars were 'piled with skulls' — state BOTH the artistic mastery AND the brutal context plainly, no editorial. Repatriation is a fact, not an editorial verdict (avoid current-politics drift).

topics.name: Pre-Columbian monumental art (Maya / Aztec / Moai)
topics.scope: Mayan temples; Aztec calendar stone; Easter Island heads
topics.source: AP Art History (Indigenous Americas, Pacific); Core Knowledge
topics.framing_note: New-World + Pacific stone traditions on their own terms (§4). Cool-fact answers: the Aztec Sun Stone packing a whole cosmology into carved rings; the Moai 'walked' upright into place (rocked side to side with ropes, as modern experiments showed). The Aztec honest-brutality record (Templo Mayor sacrifice) belongs to the monuments/civilization cells, not forced into every art question — keep THIS cell on the artistry, state context plainly where relevant.

topics.name: Gregorian chant and medieval sacred music
topics.scope: monophonic plainchant; Hildegard of Bingen; notation born
topics.framing_note: Where Western WRITTEN music begins — moral_vision §3.4 Christian-heritage thread + framework's named 'Hildegard of Bingen, Gregorian chant, Notre-Dame school polyphony.' Cool-fact answer: monks needed to remember hundreds of melodies, so they invented the staff and notation — the reason we can still play 1,000-year-old music. Hildegard = a 12th-c abbess composing visionary music + the drama-of-the-mind hook (a woman whose authority the Church recognized). On its own terms, no smug voice.

topics.name: Bach — Baroque counterpoint
topics.scope: St. Matthew Passion; fugues; revived by Mendelssohn 1829
topics.framing_note: Framework names the full arc: 'Bach (St. Matthew Passion forgotten 1727 then revived by 20-year-old Mendelssohn 1829).' High weight, foundational composer. Beauty-of-mechanism (§2): WHY the fugues feel inevitable — a single theme chased through every voice. Surprise-reversal: Bach was half-forgotten as old-fashioned until the teenage Mendelssohn resurrected the St. Matthew Passion. Cool-fact answers over 'who composed.'

topics.name: Handel — Messiah and the Hallelujah Chorus
topics.scope: oratorio; standing tradition; written in 24 days
topics.framing_note: Framework names 'Handel's Hallelujah Chorus.' Most-performed choral work, instantly familiar. Cool-fact answers: the whole Messiah composed in about 24 days in a near-trance; the audience-standing tradition said to start when King George II rose during the Hallelujah Chorus. Present straight. Number ('24 days') only works if the stem CONSTRUCTS it as the shattered-expectation payoff (Tier-4 rule).

topics.name: Mozart — the prodigy composer
topics.scope: child genius; Don Giovanni; unfinished Requiem; died at 35
topics.framing_note: Framework names 'Mozart (prodigy, Don Giovanni, Requiem unfinished dead at 35).' Archetypal prodigy = drama-of-the-mind, high weight. Cool-fact answers: composing full symphonies before age 10 and touring Europe's courts as a child; the Requiem left unfinished at his death at 35, commissioned anonymously by a stranger he came to believe was Death itself. Mind the strict drama-available rule — ask the act/object, not a date.

topics.name: Beethoven — the deaf composer and the Ninth
topics.scope: going deaf; Fifth's four notes; Ode to Joy premiere 1824
topics.framing_note: Framework names it with the cool detail: 'Beethoven's deaf 9th-symphony premiere 1824 (contralto turned him to see the applause).' THAT is the Tier-1 Named-Things/Vivid-Action answer — he couldn't hear the ovation and had to be turned around to see it. High weight, deaf-genius drama-of-the-mind. The four-note 'fate' opening of the Fifth is the kid hook. Bridge to Romantic music.

topics.name: Romantic-era composers — Chopin, Tchaikovsky, Wagner
topics.scope: Chopin's Polish exile; 1812 Overture cannons; Wagner's Ring
topics.source: Core Knowledge music; AP Euro; cultural literacy
topics.framing_note: Framework names all three with cool details: 'Chopin (Polish exile, dying TB, buried with Polish soil), Wagner's Ring + Bayreuth, Tchaikovsky's 1812 Overture with real cannons.' Each detail is the answer: real cannons scored into the 1812; Chopin's heart removed and smuggled back to Poland in a jar; Wagner building his own opera house for one 16-hour cycle. Drama-of-the-mind + Named-Things. Ask the specific, not attribution.

topics.name: Stravinsky — Rite of Spring riot 1913
topics.scope: audience riot at the premiere; modernist rhythm
topics.framing_note: Framework names 'Stravinsky's Rite of Spring riot 1913' in BOTH Pillar 1 and Pillar 6 — the moment modern music broke from tradition. The riot IS the cool-fact answer (the audience came to BLOWS over the pounding dissonant rhythm and primitive choreography). Drama-available: the violence in the stem yields the riot, not the venue/date. Surprise-reversal: a ballet that caused a literal brawl.

topics.name: Birth of jazz — Louis Armstrong and New Orleans
topics.scope: blues roots; improvisation; Armstrong; the American art form
topics.source: Core Knowledge music (jazz explicit); cultural literacy
topics.framing_note: America's original art form — fits the celebrate-the-American-experiment thread (moral_vision §2/§3.6) at the cultural level; an achievement born of Black American musicians. Cool-fact answer: improvisation = inventing the melody live, never the same twice; Armstrong's trumpet and gravel voice making the soloist the star. Present the achievement straight, no ideology. Ask the specific.

topics.name: American vocal traditions — spirituals, folk, patriotic song
topics.scope: spirituals; folk songs; Star-Spangled Banner
topics.framing_note: The shared American songbook — celebrate-the-American-experiment thread. Cool-fact answers: spirituals like 'Wade in the Water' carrying coded escape directions for the Underground Railroad; the Star-Spangled Banner's tune borrowed from an old British drinking song; written by Francis Scott Key watching Fort McHenry survive the night (connects to War of 1812 cell). Honest record (the spirituals' slavery origin) stated plainly.

topics.name: Families of instruments and the orchestra
topics.scope: strings/brass/woodwind/percussion; Peter and the Wolf
topics.framing_note: Basic musical literacy — how orchestral music is built. Lowest weight in the strand (foundational, not a wonder keystone), but legitimate Core Knowledge. Cool-fact hook to avoid dry definition: Prokofiev's 'Peter and the Wolf' assigns each character a specific instrument (the duck = oboe, the wolf = French horns) so kids learn the families by story. Keep it kid-accessible; one concrete handle.

topics.name: Homer's epics — Iliad and Odyssey
topics.scope: Trojan War; Odysseus' journey; oral epic; Western canon's start
topics.framing_note: Where Western literature BEGINS — top-billing ideas-strand keystone (Athens inheritance). High weight. Cool-fact answers: the Trojan Horse trick; Odysseus blinding the Cyclops by calling himself 'Nobody'; composed and memorized orally for centuries before being written down. The oral-memory feat = §2 ordinary-ingenuity wonder. Present straight.

topics.name: Greek drama — tragedy and comedy
topics.scope: Sophocles; Oedipus; theater of Dionysus; masks
topics.source: Core Knowledge; AP Euro; cultural literacy
topics.framing_note: Origin of Western theater — Athens-inheritance ideas keystone. Cool-fact answers: every role played by masked men, with giant masks that doubled as megaphones to carry the voice up a stone hillside seating 17,000; the same Oedipus story that gave us 'tragic flaw.' Present on its own terms, no condescension to the ancient world (§4).

topics.name: Dante — The Divine Comedy
topics.scope: Inferno's nine circles; Italian vernacular; the afterlife journey
topics.framing_note: Medieval Christian imagination's masterpiece that also SHAPED the Italian language — moral_vision §3.4 thread (Christian heritage as intellectual foundation) treated on its own terms, no smug voice (§4). Cool-fact answers: Dante wrote it in everyday Italian instead of scholarly Latin, helping fix the language; he placed his own political enemies (and a pope) into specific circles of Hell by name. The nine descending circles is the kid hook.

topics.name: Shakespeare — the plays and the language
topics.scope: Globe Theatre; Hamlet/Macbeth/Romeo; coined words
topics.framing_note: Greatest writer in English — top-billing ideas keystone, high weight. Cool-fact answers: he coined or first-recorded hundreds of words still used daily ('eyeball,' 'lonely,' 'swagger') and phrases ('wild-goose chase,' 'break the ice'); boys played all the women's roles at the Globe; the open-air theatre's 'groundlings' stood in the pit for a penny. Ask the wondrous specific, never 'who wrote' rote.

topics.name: Cervantes — Don Quixote
topics.scope: tilting at windmills; first modern novel; Spanish Golden Age
topics.framing_note: The first modern novel + an idiom kids still use ('tilting at windmills,' 'quixotic'). Spanish Golden Age. Cool-fact answer: the old knight charging windmills he believes are giants; Cervantes himself lost the use of his left hand at the Battle of Lepanto (connects to the military strand) and later wrote the book partly while imprisoned. Present straight; ask the specific.

topics.name: Mozart vs. Salieri — the poisoning myth vs. the record
topics.scope: the real Salieri (respected court composer who taught Beethoven/Schubert/Liszt, NOT a murderer); myth vs. history
topics.framing_note: Behind-the-scenes wonder REQUIRED by HISTORY_TEMPLATES §1 (popular myth vs. historical reality), applied to music. The 'Salieri poisoned Mozart' story (from the play/film Amadeus) is FALSE — Salieri was a successful, respected Vienna court composer. Tell the truer story without tearing down: the professional rivalry was real and ordinary; the murder is legend. Teaches kids that cultural narratives are constructed. Honest, not cynical (§4). Cool-fact answer = the real students he taught, or that the poisoning never happened.
topics.rationale: The framework's 'behind-the-scenes wonder — popular myth vs. historical reality' pattern is a REQUIRED question type (HISTORY_TEMPLATES §1, with worked examples like Rosa Parks/Colvin and Marie Antoinette's non-quote). The consensus Mozart/Requiem cells invite the single most famous myth-vs-record case in music, and correcting a falsehood most kids absorb from pop culture is exactly what the pattern is for.

topics.name: Shostakovich's Fifth — music coded under Stalin
topics.scope: the 1937 'forced rejoicing' finale; composing under threat of the Gulag after official denunciation
topics.framing_note: The communist-atrocity-truth-telling pillar (moral_vision §3.1; framework Pillar 4, HEAVY by design) applied to the ARTS — courage in pursuit of truth (§2). Shostakovich wrote his Fifth after Stalin's regime denounced him in Pravda and friends were vanishing into the Gulag; the 'triumphant' finale is widely heard as hollow, forced rejoicing 'under threat.' Show the artist surviving under terror — the human at the breaking point. State the Stalinist context plainly, no false equivalence. Cool-fact answer = the hidden meaning of the finale, or the denunciation that preceded it.
topics.rationale: The framework explicitly names 'Shostakovich's 5th coded under Stalin' as a Pillar-1 music topic, and it is THE keystone case of art-made-under-totalitarianism — a HEAVY, by-design vision priority (anti-totalitarianism is foundational, meta-principle 2) that the consensus list (which stops at Stravinsky 1913) entirely omits.

topics.name: Monteverdi and the birth of opera (Palestrina to Orfeo)
topics.scope: Palestrina saving polyphony at Trent; Monteverdi's 'Orfeo' 1607 as the first enduring opera
topics.framing_note: Fills the Renaissance/early-Baroque MUSIC gap between Gregorian chant and Bach. Cool-fact answers: the legend that Palestrina's Mass single-handedly persuaded the Council of Trent NOT to ban complex polyphony from church (saving a whole musical tradition); Monteverdi's Orfeo turning the Greek Orpheus myth into the first opera still staged today. Christian-heritage music thread (§3.4) + Greek-myth-revival thread, both on their own terms.
topics.rationale: HISTORY_TEMPLATES Pillar 1 explicitly names 'Josquin, Palestrina, Monteverdi's Orfeo (first opera)' as required music content, and the consensus music sequence jumps straight from medieval chant to Bach — leaving the entire Renaissance birth-of-opera span (a named framework requirement) uncovered.

topics.name: Eiffel Tower — the structure Paris planned to tear down
topics.scope: 1889 World's Fair iron tower; the artists' petition against it; built to be temporary
topics.framing_note: Framework explicitly names 'Eiffel Tower 1889 (planned for demolition).' Surprise-reversal wonder (§2): the most beloved monument in France was built as a temporary fair exhibit, denounced by leading artists and writers as a hideous iron eyesore, and slated for demolition after 20 years — saved only because its height made it useful as a radio/wireless antenna. Engineering-as-art crossover. Cool-fact answer = the 'planned to be torn down, saved by radio' reveal.
topics.rationale: The framework names the Eiffel Tower with its signature cool fact in the Pillar-1 art/architecture list, and the consensus strand has no 19th-century iron-architecture / engineering-as-art keystone at all. It is on-strand (a named architectural keystone with an ideas-revolution hook) and carries a textbook Wonder-Pattern surprise-reversal.
